title: Active & Passive Voice
summary: Two voice conversions per shift, built from an eight-row tense table and five named fault classes. Learn the table once — simple present to future perfect, being vs been slots, modal + be + V3, the Let-anchor for imperatives and By-whom order for questions — and both directions (active→passive, passive→active) become 25-second kills.

subtopics.title: Voice basics: the three moves
subtopics.concept: In the **active voice** the subject does the action. In the **passive voice** the subject receives it. Three moves turn any active sentence into a passive one: the object becomes the subject, the verb becomes *be + V3*, and the old subject goes behind *by*. Only verbs that take an object can be made passive.

tricks.title: Tense handover
tricks.body: The helping verb must carry the original tense: wrote becomes was, writes becomes is, will write becomes will be, has written becomes has been. A changed tense in an option is a planted error.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The clerk wrote the report.*
steps: *Wrote* is simple past.
The helping verb must be *was*.
The main verb is V3: written.
example.answer: The report was written by the clerk.

tricks.title: V3-only law
tricks.body: After be, been or being, the main verb is always V3 (written, given, built). Options like *is wrote* and *was build* are wrong on sight.

tricks.title: Pronoun mirror
tricks.body: The subject pronoun becomes the object pronoun behind by (he becomes him). The object pronoun becomes the subject pronoun in front (me becomes I).

example.q: Select the passive form: *She helped me.*
steps: *Me* moves to the front, so it becomes *I*.
*She* goes behind by, so it becomes *her*.
*Helped* is simple past: *was helped*.
example.answer: I was helped by her.

mistakes.wrong: Changing the tense while converting, for example *is written* for *wrote*.
mistakes.right: Match the row: *wrote* becomes *was written*, *writes* becomes *is written*.

mistakes.wrong: Writing *by he* or *by they* in the by-phrase.
mistakes.right: Use the object case behind by: *by him*, *by them*.

mistakes.wrong: Writing *is wrote* or *was build* after be.
mistakes.right: The main verb after be is always V3: *is written*, *was built*.

mistakes.wrong: Trying to make a passive from *sleep, arrive, die, cry*.
mistakes.right: These verbs take no object, so they have no passive.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting that verb + preposition can be passive: *They laughed at him*.
mistakes.right: Move the whole unit: *He was laughed at by them*.

subtopics.notes:
### What voice means
Voice tells you who is in front: the doer or the receiver.

- **Active:** *The chef prepared the meal.* The chef (doer) is the subject.
- **Passive:** *The meal was prepared by the chef.* The meal (receiver) is the subject.

Both sentences describe the same event. Only the order changes.

### The three moves
Use these moves for every conversion. Take *The postman rings the bell.*

1. **Object becomes subject.** Find the thing the verb acts on. *The bell* is the new subject.
2. **Verb becomes be + V3.** V3 is the past participle (written, prepared, rung). Keep the tense. *Rings* is simple present, so use *is*: *is rung*.
3. **Old subject goes behind by.** Use the object case: *by the postman*, *by him*, *by them*.

Result: *The bell is rung by the postman.*

> **Rule:** The tense never changes. Only the helping verb (*is, was, has been*) carries it. The main verb is always V3.

If the doer is vague (*someone, people, they*), drop the by-phrase. *Someone has stolen my purse* becomes *My purse has been stolen.*

### Pronouns change case
A subject pronoun turns into an object pronoun when it moves behind *by*. An object pronoun turns into a subject pronoun when it moves to the front.

| Subject form | Object form |
|---|---|
| I, we | me, us |
| he, she | him, her |
| they | them |

> **Example:** *He helps me.* becomes *I am helped by him.* Now *me* is the subject, so it becomes *I*. And *he* is behind *by*, so it becomes *him*.

*By he* and *us were invited* are never correct.

### Only some verbs have a passive
A passive needs an object to move to the front. Verbs with no object have no passive: *sleep, arrive, die, cry, go, laugh*. *The baby slept peacefully* cannot become passive.

- A verb plus a preposition can work as one unit. *They laughed at him* becomes *He was laughed at.*
- Stative verbs (*have, own, resemble, lack, suit, cost*) normally refuse the passive.

> **Watch:** Test the whole phrase, not the bare verb. *Laugh* alone fails. *Laugh at* works.

### The tense table
Learn this table as one block. Take *She writes a letter.*

| Tense | Active | Passive |
|---|---|---|
| Simple present | writes | is / are + V3 |
| Present continuous | is writing | is / are being + V3 |
| Present perfect | has written | has / have been + V3 |
| Simple past | wrote | was / were + V3 |
| Past continuous | was writing | was / were being + V3 |
| Past perfect | had written | had been + V3 |
| Simple future | will write | will be + V3 |
| Future perfect | will have written | will have been + V3 |
| Going to | is going to write | is going to be + V3 |

No row has *is been*, *will being*, or a bare V1 or V2 after *be*.

### Three checks on the options
1. **Did the tense change?** *Is written* for *wrote* is wrong. Compare the option with the table row.
2. **Is the verb after be a V3?** *Is wrote* and *must obeyed* are wrong.
3. **Is the pronoun case right?** *By he* and *us were invited* are wrong.

In a well-set question, each wrong option breaks exactly one of these checks. The right option breaks none.

> **Tip:** Say the tense row aloud first. Then read the options. Do not choose by what sounds smooth.

patterns.name: Three-move conversion with a pronoun swap
patterns.howToSpot: A short active sentence. The options are passive versions that differ in the verb or in *by he / by him*.
steps: Find the object and make it the subject.
Rebuild the verb as be + V3 in the same tense.
Put the old subject behind by, in the object case.
Match is/are/was/were to the new subject.
patterns.why: Every passive sentence uses these moves, and each wrong option botches one of them.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The peon rings the bell.*
steps: The object is *the bell*, so it becomes the subject.
*Rings* is simple present, so use *is rung*.
The doer goes behind by: *by the peon*.
example.answer: The bell is rung by the peon.

patterns.name: Vague agent drops out
patterns.howToSpot: The active subject is someone, people, they or one. The right option has no by-phrase.
steps: Check whether the doer is a named person or thing.
If the doer is vague, drop it.
Keep the tense row unchanged.
patterns.why: English drops doers that add no information.

example.q: Select the passive form: *Someone has switched off the fans.*
steps: *Has switched off* is present perfect.
The passive row is *have been + V3*, and the new subject *the fans* is plural.
*Someone* is vague, so drop it.
example.answer: The fans have been switched off.

patterns.name: Pronoun-case elimination
patterns.howToSpot: Pronouns sit on both sides of the verb (he ... me, they ... us). The options mix I/me, he/him, we/us.
steps: Decide each pronoun's new job.
A pronoun moving behind by takes the object case.
A pronoun moving to the front takes the subject case.
Reject any option where either pronoun is wrong.
patterns.why: *By he* and *me was helped* are impossible, so case alone can settle the question.

example.q: Select the passive form: *They invited us to the wedding.*
steps: *Us* moves to the front and becomes *we*.
*They* goes behind by and becomes *them*.
*Invited* is simple past: *were invited*.
example.answer: We were invited to the wedding by them.

patterns.name: Sentence that cannot be made passive
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks which sentence cannot be changed into the passive. The options mix verbs with and without objects.
steps: Underline the verb in each option.
Ask: does the verb act on a thing?
A verb with no object (sleep, arrive, die) has no passive.
Stative verbs like resemble also refuse the passive.
patterns.why: The passive moves the object to the front. With no object, nothing can move.

example.q: Which sentence cannot be changed into the passive voice? (a) *The baby slept peacefully.* (b) *The mother woke the baby.* (c) *The doctor examined the reports.* (d) *The nurse weighed the newborn.*
steps: Option (a): *slept* has no object.
Options (b), (c) and (d) have objects: the baby, the reports, the newborn.
So only (a) has no passive.
example.answer: The baby slept peacefully.

patterns.name: Verb + preposition passive
patterns.howToSpot: The verb is followed by a preposition (laugh at, look after, rely on). The options move only the verb or the whole phrase.
steps: Treat verb + preposition as one unit.
The word after the preposition becomes the subject.
Keep the preposition after the passive verb.
Put the old subject behind by.
patterns.why: The preposition stays with its verb, so the passive ends with it.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The villagers relied on the doctor.*
steps: *Relied on* works as one unit.
*The doctor* becomes the subject.
*Relied* is simple past: *was relied on*.
example.answer: The doctor was relied on by the villagers.

revision: Three moves: object becomes subject; verb becomes be + V3 in the same tense; subject goes behind by.
Vague doers (someone, people, they) usually disappear from the passive.
he becomes him, she becomes her, they becomes them behind by. me becomes I in front.
No object means no passive: sleep, arrive, die, cry.
Stative verbs (have, own, resemble, lack, suit, cost) normally refuse the passive.
Options break one rule each: tense, V3, being/been, or pronoun case.

subtopics.title: Tense-by-tense conversions in action
subtopics.concept: Every voice question is one row of the tense table. First name the active tense. Then write its passive row. Then make *is/are, was/were, has/have* agree with the **new** subject. The words *being* and *been* sit in fixed places, and mixing them is the most common planted error.

tricks.title: Row recall
tricks.body: Name the active tense. Then say its passive row: present continuous is is/are being + V3, past perfect is had been + V3, future is will be + V3. Each wrong option breaks one cell of the row.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The workers had painted the gate.*
steps: *Had painted* is past perfect.
The row is *had been + V3*.
The new subject is *the gate*.
example.answer: The gate had been painted by the workers.

tricks.title: Agreement sweep
tricks.body: After converting, check is/are, was/were and has/have against the NEW subject before anything else.

tricks.title: Being or been in one look
tricks.body: Continuous in the active gives being. Perfect in the active gives been. A modal gives plain be.

mistakes.wrong: Writing *is been* for a continuous passive.
mistakes.right: Use *is being*: *The bridge is being repaired*.

mistakes.wrong: Writing *is being* for a perfect passive.
mistakes.right: Use *has been*: *The bridge has been repaired*.

mistakes.wrong: Keeping the old subject's number: *The returns has been filed*.
mistakes.right: The new subject decides: *The returns have been filed*.

mistakes.wrong: Promoting the person and keeping the old subject: *The cook was made dinner by...*
mistakes.right: Move only one object to the front: *Dinner was made by the cook*.

mistakes.wrong: Dropping *to* in the thing-first passive: *Homework was given the students*.
mistakes.right: Write *Homework was given to the students*.

mistakes.wrong: Trying to passivise *have, own, resemble, suit*.
mistakes.right: These stative verbs normally have no passive.

subtopics.notes:
### One row at a time
Name the active tense. Then write the passive row for it.

| Active | Passive | Example |
|---|---|---|
| writes | is / are + V3 | *Ram writes a story.* becomes *A story is written by Ram.* |
| is writing | is / are being + V3 | *Sita is drawing a map.* becomes *A map is being drawn by Sita.* |
| has written | has / have been + V3 | *They have caught the thief.* becomes *The thief has been caught.* |
| wrote | was / were + V3 | *The cook made dinner.* becomes *Dinner was made by the cook.* |
| was writing | was / were being + V3 | *The boys were flying kites.* becomes *Kites were being flown by the boys.* |
| had written | had been + V3 | *She had finished the work.* becomes *The work had been finished by her.* |
| will write | will be + V3 | *The PM will address the nation.* becomes *The nation will be addressed by the PM.* |
| will have written | will have been + V3 | *He will have completed it.* becomes *It will have been completed.* |

### Being or been
Two small words cause many errors. Each has one fixed place.

- **Continuous tense** in the active means **being**: *is being built, was being built.*
- **Perfect tense** in the active means **been**: *has been taken, had been taken, will have been taken.*
- **Modal** (will, can, must) means plain **be**: *will be published, must be obeyed.*

> **Rule:** *Being* follows a continuous *be*. *Been* follows *have* or *had*. Never write *is been* or *will being*.

### Agree with the new subject
After you convert, the new subject decides *is/are, was/were, has/have*. The old subject no longer matters.

*They have completed the projects.* The new subject is *the projects*. So write *The projects have been completed.*

*The clerk has filed the returns.* The new subject is plural. So write *The returns have been filed by the clerk*, not *has been*.

> **Watch:** Every set of options has one choice that agrees with the old subject. Check agreement first.

### Verbs with two objects
Give, send, offer, grant, show, teach and award take two objects: a person and a thing. So they have two passives.

*The teacher gave the students homework.*

- Person first: *The students were given homework.*
- Thing first: *Homework was given to the students.*

The person-first form is usually the keyed answer. The thing-first form needs *to*. *Homework was given the students* is wrong.

### Tenses that have no passive row
Present perfect continuous (*has been writing*), past perfect continuous (*had been writing*) and future continuous (*will be writing*) have no passive row in these exams. If a question uses one, look for the nearest simple form. Do not invent *is being been written*.

### Stative verbs
*Have, own, possess, resemble, lack, suit, fit* and *cost* are normally stative. They describe a state, not an action. *A car is had by him* is not English. When a question uses one of these verbs, look for a "no passive possible" answer.

patterns.name: Perfect-row passives (has/had/will have been + V3)
patterns.howToSpot: The active verb is *has written*, *had written* or *will have written*. The options differ in *been*, the helping verb or the tense.
steps: Name the active tense: present, past or future perfect.
Write its row: has/have been, had been, will have been + V3.
Match the helping verb to the new subject.
Keep the doer behind by, in the object case.
patterns.why: Perfect rows are set most often, and each wrong option breaks one cell.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The workers have painted the gate.*
steps: *Have painted* is present perfect.
The row is *has/have been + V3*.
The new subject *the gate* is singular, so use *has*.
example.answer: The gate has been painted by the workers.

patterns.name: Continuous-row passives (is/are/was/were being + V3)
patterns.howToSpot: The active verb is *is/are/was/were + V-ing*. The options mix *being*, *been* and the bare participle.
steps: Continuous in the active means *being* in the passive.
Match is/are or was/were to the new subject.
Reject options that drop *being*.
patterns.why: *Being* marks the continuous tense. Without it, the tense has changed.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The masons are laying the bricks.*
steps: *Are laying* is present continuous.
The row is *is/are being + V3*.
The new subject *the bricks* is plural, so use *are*.
example.answer: The bricks are being laid by the masons.

patterns.name: Re-agreement with the new subject
patterns.howToSpot: The active subject is plural and the object is singular, or the reverse. One option agrees with the old subject.
steps: Move the object to the front and note its number.
Singular subject: is, was, has. Plural subject: are, were, have.
Then check the rest of the row.
patterns.why: The helping verb follows its own subject, and the subject has changed.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The clerk has filed all the returns.*
steps: The new subject is *all the returns*, which is plural.
*Has filed* is present perfect: *have been + V3*.
*Has been filed* would agree with the old subject.
example.answer: All the returns have been filed by the clerk.

patterns.name: Being or been slot
patterns.howToSpot: The options are the same except for *being* and *been* (is being repaired / is been repaired).
steps: Name the active tense: continuous or perfect.
Continuous means being. Perfect means been. Modal means neither.
Check that the helping verb has the same tense as the active verb.
patterns.why: *Being* and *been* have fixed places, so swapping them is a common planted error.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The engineers were repairing the bridge when we crossed.*
steps: *Were repairing* is past continuous.
The row is *was/were being + V3*.
The new subject *the bridge* is singular, so use *was*.
example.answer: The bridge was being repaired when we crossed.

patterns.name: Two-object verb: person-first passive
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has a person and a thing after give, grant, show, offer or award. One option starts with the person.
steps: Find the person and the thing.
The keyed passive moves the person to the front.
If an option moves the thing first, it must keep *to* before the person.
patterns.why: Both passives are correct. The setter breaks the thing-first one by deleting *to*.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The principal granted Meena a scholarship.*
steps: The person is *Meena*. The thing is *a scholarship*.
Person first: *Meena was granted a scholarship by the principal.*
*A scholarship was granted Meena* has no *to*, so it is broken.
example.answer: Meena was granted a scholarship by the principal.

patterns.name: Verbs that refuse the passive
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks which sentence cannot be made passive. One option uses have, own, resemble, lack or suit.
steps: Underline each option's verb.
Stative verbs (resemble, lack, suit, have) do not passivise.
Verbs with a normal object do.
patterns.why: A stative verb describes a state, so no receiver can move to the front.

example.q: Which sentence cannot be changed into the passive voice? (a) *The manager signed the letter.* (b) *The girl resembles her mother.* (c) *The clerk typed the notice.* (d) *Rahul opened the door.*
steps: *Signed, typed* and *opened* are action verbs with objects.
*Resembles* is a stative verb.
*Her mother resembles by the girl* is not English.
example.answer: The girl resembles her mother.

revision: Perfect rows: has/have been, had been, will have been + V3.
Continuous rows: is/are/was/were being + V3.
Modals: modal + be + V3, with nothing between.
being follows a continuous be. been follows have or had. Never is been, never will being.
The new subject decides is/are, was/were, has/have.
Two-object verbs: person-first passive is keyed; thing-first needs *to*.
No passive row: present perfect continuous, past perfect continuous, future continuous.

subtopics.title: Modals, imperatives, infinitives and questions
subtopics.concept: Modals (will, can, must, should) follow one row: **modal + be + V3**. Orders use **Let + object + be + V3**. Requests, advice and warnings use *You are requested / advised / warned to*. Questions start with *By whom* or move the question word to the front.

tricks.title: Let anchor
tricks.body: An order (no subject, base verb) points to Let + object + be + V3. An option with no Let and no modal cannot be right.

example.q: Select the passive form: *Switch off the mobile.*
steps: It is an order with a base verb.
Use Let + object + be + V3.
*Switch off* becomes *switched off*.
example.answer: Let the mobile be switched off.

tricks.title: By whom first
tricks.body: Who-questions become *By whom + was/were/is + new subject + V3*. Check the word order first, because options scramble it.

tricks.title: Frame words
tricks.body: Please gives *You are requested to*. Advice gives *You are advised to*. A warning gives *You are warned not to*.

mistakes.wrong: Changing *Please help me* into *Let me be helped*.
mistakes.right: Use the request frame: *You are requested to help me*.

mistakes.wrong: Writing *By whom this was written?*
mistakes.right: Use question order: *By whom was this written?*

mistakes.wrong: Dropping *to* in the second passive of a two-object verb: *Homework was given the students*.
mistakes.right: Write *Homework was given to the students*.

mistakes.wrong: Putting *being* or *been* after a modal: *must been obeyed*.
mistakes.right: Write modal + be + V3: *must be obeyed*.

mistakes.wrong: Writing *Let the gate be open*.
mistakes.right: After *be*, use V3: *Let the gate be opened*.

subtopics.notes:
### Modals have one row
Will, shall, can, could, may, might, must, should and ought to all follow **modal + be + V3**.

- *You must obey the rules.* becomes *The rules must be obeyed.*
- *They can solve it.* becomes *It can be solved.*
- *Ought to* keeps its *to*: *The bill ought to be paid.*

> **Rule:** Nothing goes between the modal and *be*. *Must being obeyed* and *must been obeyed* are wrong.

### Orders use Let
An order has no subject and starts with a base verb. Convert it with **Let + object + be + V3**.

- Order: *Shut the door.* becomes *Let the door be shut.*
- Negative order: *Do not pluck the flowers.* becomes *Let the flowers not be plucked.* You can also write *The flowers should not be plucked.*
- The verb after *be* is always V3. Write *Let the gate be opened*, never *be open* or *be opening*.

### Requests, advice and warnings
Polite words change the frame. The rest of the sentence stays the same.

| Active sentence | Passive frame | Example |
|---|---|---|
| please / kindly | You are requested to + V1 | *Please post this letter.* becomes *You are requested to post this letter.* |
| advice | You are advised to + V1 | *Give up smoking.* becomes *You are advised to give up smoking.* |
| danger, warning | You are warned not to + V1 | *Never touch the wire.* becomes *You are warned not to touch the wire.* |

> **Tip:** Please means requested. Advice means advised. Danger means warned.

### Questions come in three shapes
1. **Who as doer.** Use *By whom + auxiliary + new subject + V3*. *Who broke the window?* becomes *By whom was the window broken?*
2. **Whom or what as receiver.** The question word becomes the subject. *Whom did the manager appoint?* becomes *Who was appointed by the manager?*
3. **Yes/no question.** Put the helping verb first. *Did she sing a song?* becomes *Was a song sung by her?*

> **Watch:** Question order puts the helping verb before the subject. *By whom the window was broken?* is statement order and is wrong.

### Infinitives and gerunds
- **Infinitive:** *to write* becomes *to be written*. *I want someone to compile the report* becomes *I want the report to be compiled.*
- **Gerund:** *writing* becomes *being written*. *He likes people praising him* becomes *He likes being praised.*

After *like, hate, want* use *being* or *to be*. Never use *been* there.

### Verbs with two objects
*Give, send, offer, teach, show* and *tell* have two passives. *The guide showed the tourists the paintings* becomes:

- *The tourists were shown the paintings by the guide.* (clean)
- *The paintings were shown to the tourists.* (needs *to*)

*The paintings were shown the tourists* is broken.

patterns.name: Modal + be + V3
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has will, can, must, should or ought to. The options add being, been or drop be.
steps: Spot the modal and keep it unchanged.
Use the fixed row: modal + be + V3.
Reject options with being, been or a missing be.
patterns.why: The modal row has no variants, so any option that changes it is wrong.

example.q: Select the passive form: *You should check the receipts.*
steps: *Should* is a modal and stays.
Use *should be + V3*.
The new subject is *the receipts*.
example.answer: The receipts should be checked.

patterns.name: Order becomes Let + object + be + V3
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence is a bare order with a base verb and no subject. The right option starts with Let.
steps: Spot the order (no subject, base verb).
Write Let + object + be + V3.
Reject options with no Let, and options with V1 or V-ing after be.
patterns.why: Let is the standard passive frame for an order.

example.q: Select the passive form: *Post this letter today.*
steps: It is an order with a base verb.
The object is *this letter*.
Use Let + object + be + V3.
example.answer: Let this letter be posted today.

patterns.name: Negative order and warning
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence says *Do not ...* or *Never ...*. The options must keep *not* in the right place.
steps: Decide the tone: request, advice or warning.
Use requested / advised / warned not to + V1.
For a bare negative order, use Let + object + not + be + V3.
Put *not* before *to*: *not to smoke*.
patterns.why: The negative travels with the frame, so options that drop the frame fail.

example.q: Select the passive form: *Please do not smoke in the hall.*
steps: It is a polite request.
Use *You are requested not to + V1*.
Keep the rest: *smoke in the hall*.
example.answer: You are requested not to smoke in the hall.

patterns.name: Request: You are requested to
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has *please* or *kindly* and a base verb. The right option starts with *You are requested to*.
steps: Spot please or kindly.
Start with *You are requested to*.
Keep the rest of the sentence word for word.
Treat Let-forms as decoys.
patterns.why: *Please* cannot stay in a passive clause, so the frame *requested to* replaces it.

example.q: Select the passive form: *Kindly grant me a day's leave.*
steps: *Kindly* signals a request.
Use *You are requested to + V1*.
Keep *grant me a day's leave*.
example.answer: You are requested to grant me a day's leave.

patterns.name: Question conversions (By whom / Who was)
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence ends with a question mark. A who-question needs *By whom*. A whom or what question moves the question word to the front.
steps: Decide the question word's job: doer or receiver.
Doer: By whom + auxiliary + new subject + V3.
Receiver: the question word becomes the subject.
Check that the helping verb comes before the subject.
patterns.why: Most errors here are word-order errors, not verb-form errors.

example.q: Select the passive form: *Who broke the window?*
steps: *Who* is the doer, so start with *By whom*.
*Broke* is simple past: *was + V3*.
The new subject is *the window*.
example.answer: By whom was the window broken?

patterns.name: Infinitive and gerund passives
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has *to + verb* after want, or a gerund after like or hate. The options offer to be, being and been.
steps: Infinitive: to + V1 becomes to be + V3.
Gerund: V-ing becomes being + V3.
Reject *been* after like or want.
Reject options that keep the old doer.
patterns.why: The passive marker takes the same slot the active verb held.

example.q: Select the passive form: *He likes people praising him.*
steps: *Praising* is a gerund.
The gerund passive is *being + V3*.
The doer *people* drops out.
example.answer: He likes being praised.

patterns.name: Advice and warning frames
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence gives advice (Give up, Avoid) or a danger warning (Never touch). The options use advised or warned.
steps: Advice: You are advised to + V1.
Warning about danger: You are warned not to + V1.
Keep the rest of the sentence unchanged.
patterns.why: The frame word matches the tone: requested, advised or warned.

example.q: Select the passive form: *Never touch the live wire.*
steps: *Never touch* is a warning about danger.
Use *You are warned not to + V1*.
Keep *touch the live wire*.
example.answer: You are warned not to touch the live wire.

revision: Modal row: modal + be + V3. No being, no been. Ought to keeps its to.
Order: Let + object + be + V3. Negative: Let ... not be ... or should not be.
please: You are requested to. advice: You are advised to. danger: You are warned not to.
Who question: By whom + auxiliary + new subject + V3.
Whom or what question: the question word becomes the subject (Who was appointed...?).
Yes/no question: helping verb first (Was a song sung by her?).
to write becomes to be written. people praising becomes being praised.

subtopics.title: Reverse conversions: passive to active
subtopics.concept: To go back from passive to active, move the doer to the front and rebuild the tense. Read the **first helping verb**, not the participle, to find the tense. If no doer is given, use *they*. The old subject leaves in the object case.

tricks.title: First helping verb
tricks.body: Read only the first helping verb. Was means past. Is means present. Has or had means perfect. Will means future. Is being and was being mean continuous.

example.q: Select the active form: *The walls had been whitewashed by the masons.*
steps: *Had been + V3* is past perfect.
The doer is *the masons*.
Past perfect active: *had + V3*.
example.answer: The masons had whitewashed the walls.

tricks.title: Doer hunt
tricks.body: The by-phrase gives the new subject. No by-phrase means *they*, *people* or *someone*.

tricks.title: Object-case check
tricks.body: The last pronoun must be in the object case: *praised him*, not *praised he*. Many options fail exactly here.

mistakes.wrong: Taking *was being chased* back to *chased*.
mistakes.right: Keep it continuous: *were chasing*.

mistakes.wrong: Leaving the old subject in the subject slot: *The principal was praised him*.
mistakes.right: Move it behind the verb in the object case.

mistakes.wrong: Ending with a subject pronoun: *praised he*.
mistakes.right: Use the object pronoun: *praised him*.

mistakes.wrong: Changing the tense on the way back: *was written* becomes *has written*.
mistakes.right: Read the first helping verb. *Was* means simple past: *wrote*.

mistakes.wrong: Reversing the roles: *The window broke the cricketer*.
mistakes.right: The by-phrase noun is the doer: *The cricketer broke the window*.

subtopics.notes:
### The reverse run
The method mirrors the forward one. Move the doer to the front, rebuild the tense, and move the old subject behind the verb.

| Passive | Active |
|---|---|
| The letter was written by Sita. | Sita wrote the letter. |
| The road is being repaired. | They are repairing the road. |
| The work had been finished. | She had finished the work. |
| The results will be declared. | The board will declare the results. |
| The kite was being flown by the boy. | The boy was flying the kite. |

### Read the first helping verb
The participle never tells you the tense. Every passive row ends in V3. The first helping verb shows the tense.

| Passive | Active tense | Example |
|---|---|---|
| was/were + V3 | simple past | *was written* becomes *wrote* |
| is/are being + V3 | present continuous | *is being written* becomes *is writing* |
| was/were being + V3 | past continuous | *was being written* becomes *was writing* |
| has/have been + V3 | present perfect | *has been written* becomes *has written* |
| had been + V3 | past perfect | *had been written* becomes *had written* |
| will be + V3 | simple future | *will be written* becomes *will write* |
| will have been + V3 | future perfect | *will have been written* becomes *will have written* |
| modal + be + V3 | modal + V1 | *must be obeyed* becomes *must obey* |

> **Rule:** Being means continuous. If the passive has *being*, the active must have V-ing.

### Find the doer
- A by-phrase gives the new subject. *By Sita* becomes *Sita*. Keep the noun. Change only its place.
- No by-phrase? Use *they* (or *people*). *The thief was arrested last night* becomes *They arrested the thief last night.*
- Do not reverse the roles. *The window was broken by the cricketer* becomes *The cricketer broke the window*. It never becomes *The window broke the cricketer*.

### The old subject leaves in the object case
The old subject moves behind the verb, so a pronoun takes the object form.

- *She was praised by the teacher.* becomes *The teacher praised her.*
- *He was helped by his friends.* becomes *His friends helped him.*

> **Watch:** An option that ends *praised she* or *helped he* is wrong at once. Check the last word first.

### Continuous passives return to V-ing
*Was being + V3* is past continuous. The active must use *was/were + V-ing*.

*The path was being cleared by volunteers.* becomes *The volunteers were clearing the path.*

Two decoys are common. One returns the simple past (*cleared*) and loses the ongoing sense. The other changes the tense to present perfect. Reject both.

### Let and requested go back
- *Let the door be shut.* becomes *Shut the door.*
- *You are requested to post this letter.* becomes *Please post this letter.*

The frame word tells you the tone: requested means please, advised means advice, warned means danger.

patterns.name: Tense recovery from the first helping verb
patterns.howToSpot: A passive sentence with a by-phrase. The active options differ only in tense.
steps: Ignore the participle and read the first helping verb.
Map it: had been to had + V3, has been to has + V3, was being to was/were + V-ing, will be to will + V1.
Move the by-phrase noun to the subject slot.
Put the old subject after the verb.
patterns.why: Every passive row ends in V3, so only the helping verb shows the tense.

example.q: Select the active form: *The walls had been whitewashed by the masons.*
steps: *Had been + V3* is past perfect.
The doer is *the masons*.
Past perfect active: *had + V3*.
example.answer: The masons had whitewashed the walls.

patterns.name: Missing doer: supply they
patterns.howToSpot: The passive has no by-phrase. The right option starts with *They* and keeps the tense.
steps: Check that there is no by-phrase.
Put *they* in front of the rebuilt verb.
Move the passive subject to the object slot.
patterns.why: Passives often hide a vague doer. *They* is the usual stand-in.

example.q: Select the active form: *The results will be declared on Monday.*
steps: *Will be + V3* is simple future.
There is no doer, so use *they*.
Active: *will + V1*.
example.answer: They will declare the results on Monday.

patterns.name: Object-case pronoun at the end
patterns.howToSpot: The passive subject is a pronoun (he, she, they, we). The options end with the pronoun in both cases.
steps: Move the by-phrase noun to the front and rebuild the tense.
The old subject pronoun leaves in the object case: him, her, them, us.
Scan the last word of each option first.
patterns.why: This is the mirror of the forward pronoun swap.

example.q: Select the active form: *She was praised by the teacher.*
steps: *Was praised* is simple past.
The teacher is the doer.
*She* becomes *her* in the object slot.
example.answer: The teacher praised her.

patterns.name: Continuous passive returns to V-ing
patterns.howToSpot: The passive has *is/are/was/were being + V3*. One option is a plain past and another is a perfect. Only the V-ing option is right.
steps: Spot *being*: the active must have V-ing.
Match the helping verb to the tense and to the doer's number.
Keep the rest of the sentence.
patterns.why: Dropping the continuous in the active changes the meaning.

example.q: Select the active form: *The path was being cleared by the volunteers.*
steps: *Was being + V3* is past continuous.
The doer *the volunteers* is plural: *were + V-ing*.
The old subject *the path* moves after the verb.
example.answer: The volunteers were clearing the path.

patterns.name: Let and requested frames go back
patterns.howToSpot: The passive starts with *Let ... be* or *You are requested / advised / warned to*. The active options are orders or requests.
steps: Let ... be + V3 goes back to a bare order.
*Requested to* goes back to *please*.
Keep the object and the rest of the sentence.
patterns.why: The frame words are only the passive form of an order or request.

example.q: Select the active form: *You are requested to post this letter.*
steps: *Requested to* means the sentence is a polite request.
Use *please*.
Keep the verb and the object.
example.answer: Please post this letter.

revision: The doer becomes the subject. If there is no doer, use they.
Read the first helping verb: was, is being, has been, had been, will be, modal be.
The old subject leaves in the object case: praised her, helped him.
being in the passive means V-ing in the active.
modal + be + V3 goes back to modal + V1.
requested means please. Let ... be ... means a bare order.

subtopics.title: Exam strategy: the 20-second conversion protocol
subtopics.concept: A voice question takes under 30 seconds. Use the same five steps every time: tag the voice, fix the tense, move the parts, re-agree the verb, and remove the options that break a rule. Each wrong option usually breaks exactly one rule.

tricks.title: Name the fault
tricks.body: Every wrong option breaks one rule: V-form, being/been, tense, agreement or pronoun. Name the fault and the option is out.

example.q: Select the passive form: *They are constructing a new library.*
steps: *Are constructing* is present continuous.
The row is *is/are being + V3*.
The new subject *a new library* is singular.
example.answer: A new library is being constructed by them.

tricks.title: Five-row priority
tricks.body: Learn simple present, simple past, present perfect, present continuous and modals first. They cover most of the questions.

tricks.title: Write it, do not just say it
tricks.body: Voice errors hide on paper. Convert sentences in writing every day. The hand learns the pattern faster than the ear.

mistakes.wrong: Skipping the re-agreement check after conversion.
mistakes.right: Always match is/are, was/were, has/have to the new subject.

mistakes.wrong: Learning conversions word by word.
mistakes.right: Learn them as tense rows.

mistakes.wrong: Ignoring the pronoun at the end of the sentence.
mistakes.right: Check the case of every pronoun. It is the fastest way to remove an option.

mistakes.wrong: Accepting *is been* because it sounds like *is being*.
mistakes.right: Continuous means *being*. Perfect means *been*.

mistakes.wrong: Choosing the smoothest-sounding option.
mistakes.right: Compare tense row first, then being/been, then agreement, then case.

subtopics.notes:
### Why this topic is quick marks
Every voice question is one row of one table. There is no vocabulary and no guessing. Learn the rows and the marks are easy.

### The five-step protocol
1. **Tag the voice.** Active stem means build a passive. Passive stem means build an active.
2. **Fix the tense.** Read the first helping verb. Say the row aloud: *was writing* becomes *was being + V3*.
3. **Move the parts.** Object and subject swap places. The old subject goes behind by, or becomes *they* if missing. Pronouns change case.
4. **Re-agree the verb.** Match is/are, was/were, has/have to the new subject.
5. **Remove faulty options.** Name each fault.

> **Tip:** Build the correct sentence yourself before you read the options.

### The four fault classes
| Fault | What it looks like | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong V-form after be | V1 or V2 where V3 belongs | *is wrote, must obeyed, is ringed* |
| Broken being/been slot | been after a continuous be, being after have | *is been built, has being taken* |
| Tense change | the row is from another tense | *was written* for *writes* |
| Case or agreement | wrong pronoun form, or wrong verb number | *by he, The returns has been filed* |

A fifth, rarer fault is a role reversal. *The judge was acquitted by the accused* is the wrong passive of *The judge acquitted the accused.*

### Where the marks come from
Most papers set about one active-to-passive and one passive-to-active question. Voice items also appear inside error spotting and sentence improvement.

The tenses used most are simple present, simple past, present perfect, present continuous and modals. Master these five rows first. Then add past perfect and future perfect.

Orders (Let) and By-whom questions appear less often.

### When two options both look right
Compare them on one point at a time, in this order.

1. Tense row.
2. *Being* or *been*.
3. Agreement with the new subject.
4. Pronoun case.
5. Doer kept or dropped.

One of the two options will break a point. Never choose by which one sounds smoother. Wrong options are built to sound right. *Is been* sounds like *is being* when you read fast.

> **Watch:** A clean-sounding option can still have the wrong tense row. Sound is not the test. The row is.

### Daily practice
Write ten conversions a day: five plain statements, two modals, two orders and one question. Alternate directions. Write them by hand.

After a week, say the eight rows from memory before you start. Aim for full accuracy in about 25 seconds per question.

patterns.name: One clean option: fault elimination
patterns.howToSpot: There are four passive options. Each wrong one breaks a different rule (V-form, being/been, tense) and one is clean.
steps: Build the correct passive yourself before reading the options.
Scan each option for the four faults.
Name each option's fault.
The option with no fault is the answer.
patterns.why: Questions have one clean option and three single-fault options.

example.q: Select the passive form: *They are constructing a new library.*
steps: *Are constructing* is present continuous.
The row is *is/are being + V3*.
*Is been constructed* has a broken slot; *was being constructed* changes the tense.
example.answer: A new library is being constructed by them.

patterns.name: Tense trap among near-identical options
patterns.howToSpot: All four options use the same words. They differ only in the helping verb chain (is cooked / was cooked / has been cooked / is being cooked).
steps: Fix the active tense first and say its row aloud.
Pick the option that reproduces that row exactly.
Reject rows from other tenses, even if they are grammatical.
patterns.why: The setter builds correct-looking rows from neighbouring tenses. Only the row separates them.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The peon was ringing the bell.*
steps: *Was ringing* is past continuous.
The row is *was/were being + V3*.
*Was rung* is simple past; *is being rung* is present continuous.
example.answer: The bell was being rung by the peon.

patterns.name: Identify the voice of a sentence
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks which sentence is passive (or active). The four options describe the same event.
steps: Look for be/been + V3 with the receiver as subject.
V-ing after be is still active.
A by-phrase helps, but it is not required.
patterns.why: The decoy is the continuous active, which looks like a passive.

example.q: Which sentence is in the passive voice? (a) *The window was broken by the cricketer.* (b) *The cricketer broke the window.* (c) *The cricketer was breaking the window.* (d) *The cricketer has broken the window.*
steps: Option (a) has the receiver *the window* as subject.
Its verb is was + V3.
In the other options the cricketer is the doer.
example.answer: The window was broken by the cricketer.

patterns.name: Combined skeletons
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence stacks two features, such as will have written or a question with a perfect tense.
steps: Peel the outer frame first.
Modal stays. Perfect adds been. A question adds inversion.
Apply pronoun and agreement checks last.
patterns.why: A stacked item is two rows at once. Solving the outer frame first keeps you calm.

example.q: Select the passive form: *They will have published the magazine by March.*
steps: *Will have published* is future perfect.
The row is *will have been + V3*.
The new subject is *the magazine*.
example.answer: The magazine will have been published by March.

patterns.name: Role-reversal decoy
patterns.howToSpot: The options use the same words but swap who does what. One option says the receiver did the action.
steps: Find the doer and the receiver in the stem.
The doer goes behind by in the passive.
Reject the option that makes the receiver the doer.
patterns.why: A role reversal keeps the grammar clean, so only the meaning exposes it.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The judge acquitted the accused.*
steps: The doer is *the judge*. The receiver is *the accused*.
*Acquitted* is simple past: *was acquitted*.
*The judge was acquitted by the accused* reverses the roles.
example.answer: The accused was acquitted by the judge.

revision: Protocol: tag the voice, fix the tense row, move the parts, re-agree, remove faulty options.
Fault classes: wrong V-form, being/been slot, tense change, case or agreement, role reversal.
Five rows first: simple present, simple past, present perfect, present continuous, modals.
Two clean options? Test one point at a time, starting with tense.
Build your own answer before you read the options.
Write conversions daily. Voice is a hand skill.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A declarative stem in the active voice with a transitive verb; the options are be + V3 skeletons that differ in the auxiliary chain, in being/been, or in agreement with the new subject.
pyqPatterns.approach: Name the active tense and say its passive row aloud (was writing → was being + V3). Promote the object to subject, rebuild the verb from the row, re-agree is/are/was/were/has/have with the NEW subject, and move the doer behind by in the object case. Then eliminate options by fault: wrong form after be, being/been swapped, tense row changed, agreement lost.

example.q: Select the passive form: 'The workers have painted the gate.'
example.solution: Present perfect row → has/have been + V3; new subject 'the gate' is singular: *The gate **has been painted** by the workers.* 'Have been painted' agrees with the old subject — the planted fault.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem already shows be/have been + V3 and asks for the active; the options differ in the active verb's tense (gave / has given / had given / gives).
pyqPatterns.approach: Ignore the participle — every passive row ends in V3. Read the FIRST auxiliary to fix the tense (had been → past perfect, was → simple past, is being → present continuous, will be → future). Promote the by-agent to subject; if there is no agent, start with They. Let the old subject exit in the object case (she → her, we → us).

example.q: Select the active form: 'The walls had been whitewashed by the masons.'
example.solution: had been + V3 → past perfect: *The masons **had whitewashed** the walls.* 'Have whitewashed' shifts the row to present perfect — the commonest decoy.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem is an order: a base verb with no subject ('Shut the door', 'Do not pluck the flowers'); the keyed option begins with Let.
pyqPatterns.approach: Use Let + object + be + V3 for the order; for a negative order put not after the object (Let the flowers not be plucked) or switch to a modal version (should not be plucked). Reject options without Let (they turn the order into a statement) and any form after be that is not V3.

example.q: Select the passive form: 'Switch off the mobile.'
example.solution: *Let the mobile **be switched off**.* 'Let the mobile switched off' drops be; 'The mobile is switched off' is a statement, not the order.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem carries please or kindly (request), advice in command form, or a warning (Do not drink and drive); the keyed option opens with You are requested / advised / warned.
pyqPatterns.approach: Swap the polite word for its frame — please/kindly → You are requested to, advice → You are advised to, danger → You are warned not to — and keep a base verb after to. The negative sits before to: requested **not to smoke**. Everything else in the sentence crosses unchanged.

example.q: Select the passive form: 'Please post this letter today itself.'
example.solution: *You are **requested to post** this letter today itself.* The letter cannot be made the requested party, and 'to posting' breaks the frame.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem ends with a question mark; who, whom or what leads it. The options differ mainly in word order (By whom was... vs By whom the... was) and in who/whom choice.
pyqPatterns.approach: Decide the wh-word's job first. Doer (who) → By whom + auxiliary + new subject + V3, with question order (auxiliary before subject). Receiver (whom/what) → the wh-word itself is promoted to subject: Who was appointed by the manager? Check the order before the verb — order faults outnumber verb faults here.

example.q: Select the passive form: 'Who broke the window?'
example.solution: *By whom **was the window broken**?* 'By whom the window was broken?' is statement order; 'Who was broken the window' scrambles who did what.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem's subject is someone, people, they or one; one option keeps 'by someone/by them' and the keyed one drops it; the rest of the sentence is identical.
pyqPatterns.approach: Vague agents add no information, so drop them; keep specific agents (the gardener, everyone, the committee). Dropping the agent never changes the tense row — convert first, drop last. If two options differ only in the by-phrase, the shorter (agent-less) one is keyed.

example.q: Select the passive form: 'Someone has switched off the fans.'
example.solution: *The fans **have been switched off**.* Present perfect row with the vague someone dropped; 'by someone' is grammatical but never the keyed answer.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Options identical except for the slot word: is being repaired / is been repaired / was being repaired — or the stem is continuous and one option lacks being altogether.
pyqPatterns.approach: being belongs only to continuous rows (is/are/was/were being + V3); been belongs only to perfect rows (has/have/had/will have been + V3); a modal takes plain be with neither. Fix the active tense first, then pick the slot word — never by ear, because is been and is being sound alike at speed.

example.q: Select the passive form: 'The engineers were repairing the bridge.'
example.solution: Past continuous → *The bridge **was being repaired*** — being marks the continuous; 'was been repaired' puts been in a continuous slot and is impossible.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Voice fault inside a sentence (error-spotting and improvement)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The item is not a conversion but a sentence with an embedded voice fault: is been built, must obeyed, by he, a plural new subject with has been, or a passive built from an objectless verb.
pyqPatterns.approach: Sweep for the four fault classes in order: (1) wrong verb form after be (V1/V2 where V3 belongs), (2) being/been in the wrong slot, (3) tense row changed or agreement lost with the new subject, (4) pronoun case or role reversal. The part that breaks a class is the error.

example.q: 'The new scheme has being launched / by the government / without much publicity.' Find the error.
example.solution: Present perfect needs been, not being: has **been** launched. 'Has being launched' puts being in a perfect slot — the classic voice fault.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

The chef had prepared the meal.
options: The meal has been prepared by the chef.
The meal was prepared by the chef.
The meal had prepared by the chef.
The meal had been prepared by the chef.
solvedExamples.solution: Active tense = **past perfect** (had + V3). Its passive row is **had been + V3**: 'The meal had been prepared by the chef.' Option B shifts tense to present perfect; Option C drops to simple past; Option D loses 'been'.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Past perfect row: had + V3 → had been + V3. Tense never changes.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

They are building a new bridge.
options: A new bridge is building by them.
A new bridge was being built by them.
A new bridge is being built by them.
A new bridge is been built by them.
solvedExamples.solution: Present continuous → passive row **is/are being + V3**. The new subject 'a new bridge' is singular, so **is** being built. Option B commits the classic 'is been' error (been belongs to perfect tenses); C uses V1; D changes tense to past.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Continuous → being, never been: is being + V3.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

The thief was being chased by the police.
options: The police were chasing the thief.
The police were chased the thief.
The police was chasing the thief.
The police had chased the thief.
solvedExamples.solution: 'was being + V3' is the **past continuous passive** → active is **was/were + V-ing**. The new subject 'police' is plural → **were chasing**. Option B writes V2 after 'were'; C breaks number; D changes tense.
solvedExamples.shortcut: was being + V3 → were + V-ing (past continuous back-conversion).

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

She writes a letter.
options: A letter is wrote by her.
A letter was written by her.
A letter is being written by her.
A letter is written by her.
practice.solution: Simple present → **is/are + V3**. 'A letter is written by her.' B uses V2 ('wrote') after is; C changes tense to past; D changes aspect to continuous.
practice.shortcut: Simple present row: is/are + V3.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

The gardener is watering the plants.
options: The plants are watered by the gardener.
The plants are being watered by the gardener.
The plants are being water by the gardener.
The plants is being watered by the gardener.
practice.solution: Present continuous → **are being + V3** with the plural new subject 'the plants'. B uses V1; C fails number agreement (is for plants); D drops 'being', turning it into simple present.
practice.shortcut: are being + V3 — check the V3 and the number both.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

They have completed the project.
options: The project has completed by them.
The project has being completed by them.
The project have been completed by them.
The project has been completed by them.
practice.solution: Present perfect → **has/have been + V3**. The new subject 'the project' is singular → **has been completed**. B drops 'been'; C wrongly uses 'being' in a perfect slot; D agrees the verb with 'they' instead of the new subject.
practice.shortcut: Perfect row: has/have been + V3; agree with the NEW subject.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

Someone has stolen my purse.
options: My purse has stolen.
My purse was stolen by someone.
My purse is stolen by someone.
My purse has been stolen.
practice.solution: Present perfect passive: 'My purse has been stolen.' The vague agent **someone** is dropped. B misses 'been'; C and D change the tense.
practice.shortcut: Vague agents (someone/they) vanish in the passive.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

Open the gate.
options: Let the gate be open.
Let the gate be opened.
The gate is opened.
The gate be opened.
practice.solution: An imperative converts with **Let + object + be + V3**: 'Let the gate be opened.' B produces a statement, not an order; C lacks the auxiliary; D uses the adjective 'open' instead of V3 'opened'.
practice.shortcut: Imperative anchor: Let + object + be + V3.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

You must obey the rules.
options: The rules must being obeyed.
The rules must be obeyed.
The rules must be obey.
The rules must been obeyed.
practice.solution: Modal row: **modal + be + V3** — 'The rules must be obeyed.' B uses V1; C uses 'been' after a modal (been only follows have/will have); D uses 'being' where plain 'be' is required.
practice.shortcut: Modal row: modal + be + V3 — no being, no been.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

Who taught you English?
options: By whom were you taught English?
Who was taught you English?
By whom you were taught English?
Whom were taught English by you?
practice.solution: Who-questions passivise to **By whom + auxiliary + subject**: 'By whom were you taught English?' B keeps 'who' instead of 'by whom'; C uses statement word order; D scrambles the clause entirely.
practice.shortcut: Who → By whom + aux + subject; word order is the trap.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

The novel was written by Premchand.
options: Premchand was written the novel.
Premchand has written the novel.
Premchand had written the novel.
Premchand wrote the novel.
practice.solution: 'was written' → simple past active: **wrote**. B keeps the passive verb; C and D both shift the tense (present perfect, past perfect).
practice.shortcut: was + V3 → past simple (V2).

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

The letter will be posted by the clerk.
options: The clerk will be posting the letter.
The clerk would post the letter.
The clerk will post the letter.
The clerk will posted the letter.
practice.solution: 'will be + V3' → future simple active: **will post**. B uses V2 after will; C keeps passive 'be' inside the active; D shifts the modal.
practice.shortcut: will be + V3 → will + V1.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

He was praised by the principal.
options: The principal praises him.
The principal praised him.
The principal praised he.
The principal was praised him.
practice.solution: Agent → subject ('the principal'); 'was praised' → simple past **praised**; old subject moves to object case: **him**. B ends in subject-case 'he'; C keeps the passive 'was'; D changes tense to present.
practice.shortcut: By-agent becomes subject; final pronoun in object case.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

The teacher gave the students homework.
options: The students were given homework by the teacher.
The students was given homework by the teacher.
The homework was given the students by the teacher.
The students are given homework by the teacher.
practice.solution: Double-object verb: either object can lead. 'The students were given homework by the teacher' is correct (plural → were). B breaks number; C drops the preposition 'to' ('given the students' needs 'given to the students'); D changes tense.
practice.shortcut: give offers two passives; the indirect-object one keeps 'were given'.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

The committee will announce the results.
options: The results will being announced by the committee.
The results would be announced by the committee.
The results will be announced by the committee.
The results will announced by the committee.
practice.solution: Simple future → **will be + V3**. B loses 'be'; C uses 'being' after a modal; D shifts the modal (would).
practice.shortcut: Future row: will be + V3.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

The road is being repaired by the workers.
options: The workers is repairing the road.
The workers have repaired the road.
The workers are repairing the road.
The workers are repaired the road.
practice.solution: 'is being + V3' → present continuous: **are repairing** (plural subject). B writes V3 after are; C fails number; D changes tense to perfect.
practice.shortcut: is being + V3 → are + V-ing.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

Please help the poor.
options: The poor are helped.
You are request to help the poor.
You are requested to help the poor.
Let the poor helped.
practice.solution: A 'please' request converts to **You are requested to + V1**. B drops 'be' in the Let-form and loses the request tone; C gives a statement of fact; D writes the noun 'request' where V3 'requested' is needed.
practice.shortcut: please → You are requested to …; order → Let … be …

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

The gardener had planted the saplings.
options: The saplings have been planted by the gardener.
The saplings had planted by the gardener.
The saplings were planted by the gardener.
The saplings had been planted by the gardener.
practice.solution: Past perfect → **had been + V3**: 'The saplings had been planted by the gardener.' B shifts to present perfect; C drops 'been'; D drops to simple past.
practice.shortcut: had + V3 → had been + V3.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The gardener waters the plants every morning.'
options: The plants are watering by the gardener every morning.
The plants were watered by the gardener every morning.
The plants have watered by the gardener every morning.
The plants are watered by the gardener every morning.
practice.solution: Simple present row → **are + V3**: the object *the plants* becomes the subject, *waters* becomes **are watered**, and the doer moves behind **by**. 'Are watering' keeps the active form; 'were watered' shifts the tense; 'have watered' drops *been*.
practice.shortcut: Row chant: waters → is/are watered. Then swap and add by.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The children are making a noise in the class.'
options: A noise is been made by the children in the class.
A noise is being made by the children in the class.
A noise is making by the children in the class.
A noise was being made by the children in the class.
practice.solution: Present continuous row → **is being + V3**: *a noise* is promoted, *are making* becomes **is being made** (the new subject is singular), and *the children* takes **by**. 'Is been made' puts been in a continuous slot; 'is making' stays active; 'was being made' changes the tense.
practice.shortcut: Active -ing → passive being + V3. Been never follows a continuous be.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The judge acquitted the accused of all charges.'
options: The judge was acquitted of all charges by the accused.
The accused is acquitted of all charges by the judge.
The accused was acquitted of all charges by the judge.
The accused had acquitted of all charges by the judge.
practice.solution: *The accused* is the receiver, so it becomes the subject: **was acquitted of all charges by the judge**. Promoting *the judge* instead reverses the roles of the courtroom; 'is acquitted' changes the tense; 'had acquitted' drops *been*.
practice.shortcut: Promote the RECEIVER, never the doer.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Someone has plucked my roses.'
options: My roses have been plucked.
My roses have been plucked by someone.
My roses has been plucked.
My roses had been plucked.
practice.solution: Present perfect row → **have been + V3**, and the vague agent *someone* is dropped: *My roses have been plucked.* The keyed answer never drags 'by someone' along; 'has been plucked' fails to agree with the plural *roses*; 'had been plucked' shifts to past perfect.
practice.shortcut: someone/they/people vanish in the passive.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'People speak Hindi all over northern India.'
options: Hindi is spoken by people all over northern India.
Hindi was spoken all over northern India.
Hindi is spoken all over northern India.
Hindi is speak all over northern India.
practice.solution: The vague doer *people* is dropped: **Hindi is spoken all over northern India.** Keeping 'by people' is the classic planted extra; 'was spoken' changes the tense; 'is speak' uses V1 where V3 belongs.
practice.shortcut: People as doer → drop it, convert, done.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'They will cancel the match if it rains.'
options: The match will be cancel if it rains.
The match will be cancelled if it rains.
The match would be cancelled if it rains.
The match will been cancelled if it rains.
practice.solution: Future row: **will be + V3** — *The match will be cancelled if it rains.* The vague *they* disappears; the if-clause stays untouched. 'Will be cancel' lacks the participle; 'would be cancelled' downgrades the modal; 'will been cancelled' breaks the slot (been never follows a bare modal).
practice.shortcut: Modal row: modal + be + V3. Nothing between modal and be.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'He teaches us grammar.'
options: Us are taught grammar by him.
We are taught grammar by him.
We are taught grammar by he.
We are teach grammar by him.
practice.solution: The receiver *us* is promoted to the subject form **we**, and the doer *he* slips into object case behind **by him**: *We are taught grammar by him.* 'Us are taught' keeps object case in the subject slot; 'by he' refuses the case swap; 'are teach' drops the participle.
practice.shortcut: Subject and by-agent swap cases: us→we, he→him.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'They have elected him president.'
options: He has been elected president by them.
He has been elected president.
Him has been elected president.
He has been elect president.
practice.solution: Present perfect row with the vague *they* dropped: **He has been elected president.** The pronoun *him* is promoted to subject case **he**. 'By them' is the planted vague agent; 'Him has been elected' keeps object case in the subject slot; 'has been elect' lacks the participle.
practice.shortcut: Promoted pronoun takes subject case: him→he.

practice.q: Which one of the following sentences CANNOT be changed into the passive voice?
options: The mother sang a lullaby.
The nurse fed the baby.
The baby slept peacefully on the cot.
The father bought a cradle.
practice.solution: *Slept* takes no object — there is nothing to promote, so *The baby slept peacefully on the cot* has no passive at all. The other three sentences each carry an object (*a lullaby*, *the baby*, *a cradle*) and convert cleanly.
practice.shortcut: No object → no passive. Test the verb, not the looks.

practice.q: Which one of the following sentences cannot be converted into the passive voice?
options: My uncle owns two flats in Pune.
My uncle has sold a flat in Pune.
My uncle is renting out a flat in Pune.
My uncle built two flats in Pune.
practice.solution: *Own* is a verb of possession; English does not passivise it — there is no accepted '*Two flats are owned by my uncle*'. *Sell*, *rent out* and *build* are action verbs with objects, so the other three sentences passivise normally.
practice.shortcut: Have/own/possess/resemble/lack/suit → no passive.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The students have cleaned the auditorium.'
options: The auditorium have been cleaned by the students.
The auditorium has being cleaned by the students.
The auditorium is cleaned by the students.
The auditorium has been cleaned by the students.
practice.solution: Present perfect row → **has/have been + V3**; the new subject *the auditorium* is singular, so **has been cleaned by the students**. 'Have been cleaned' agrees with the old subject; 'has being cleaned' puts being in a perfect slot; 'is cleaned' switches to the simple present row.
practice.shortcut: Perfect active → has/have been + V3. Agree with the NEW subject.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The hunters had trapped the leopard before dawn.'
options: The leopard has been trapped by the hunters before dawn.
The leopard had being trapped by the hunters before dawn.
The leopard had been trapped by the hunters before dawn.
The leopard was trapped by the hunters before dawn.
practice.solution: Past perfect row → **had been + V3**: *The leopard had been trapped by the hunters before dawn.* 'Has been trapped' lifts the row to present perfect; 'had being trapped' inserts being into a perfect slot; 'was trapped' drops to the simple past row.
practice.shortcut: had + V3 → had been + V3. The had never moves.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The chef is preparing a special dish for the guests.'
options: A special dish is prepared by the chef for the guests.
A special dish is been prepared by the chef for the guests.
A special dish is being prepared by the chef for the guests.
A special dish was being prepared by the chef for the guests.
practice.solution: Present continuous row → **is being + V3**: *A special dish is being prepared by the chef for the guests.* 'Is prepared' turns the ongoing act into a habit; 'is been prepared' breaks the continuous slot; 'was being prepared' shifts the row to past continuous.
practice.shortcut: Active is + V-ing → passive is being + V3.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The farmers were harvesting the paddy when it began to rain.'
options: The paddy was harvested by the farmers when it began to rain.
The paddy was being harvested by the farmers when it began to rain.
The paddy is being harvested by the farmers when it began to rain.
The paddy was being harvest by the farmers when it began to rain.
practice.solution: Past continuous row → **was being + V3**: *The paddy was being harvested by the farmers when it began to rain.* 'Was harvested' loses the ongoing sense; 'is being harvested' jumps tenses mid-sentence; 'was being harvest' lacks the participle.
practice.shortcut: were + V-ing → was/were being + V3.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The mayor has inaugurated the new flyovers.'
options: The new flyovers has been inaugurated by the mayor.
The new flyovers have been inaugurated by the mayor.
The new flyovers have being inaugurated by the mayor.
The new flyovers had been inaugurated by the mayor.
practice.solution: The new subject *the new flyovers* is plural, so the perfect row reads **have been inaugurated by the mayor**. 'Has been inaugurated' copies the old subject's number; 'have being inaugurated' breaks the slot; 'had been inaugurated' changes the tense.
practice.shortcut: After promoting, re-agree: flyovers → have, not has.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The committee has approved these proposals.'
options: These proposals has been approved by the committee.
These proposals have approved by the committee.
These proposals were approved by the committee.
These proposals have been approved by the committee.
practice.solution: New subject *these proposals* is plural → **have been approved by the committee**. 'Has been approved' forgets to re-agree; 'have approved by' drops *been*; 'were approved' moves the row to the simple past.
practice.shortcut: Plural new subject → have been, never has been.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The mechanics were repairing my scooter.'
options: My scooter was been repaired by the mechanics.
My scooter was being repaired by the mechanics.
My scooter is being repaired by the mechanics.
My scooter was repairing by the mechanics.
practice.solution: Past continuous row → **was being repaired by the mechanics** — being marks the continuous, been never does. 'Was been repaired' swaps the slot word; 'is being repaired' leaves the past; 'was repairing' keeps the active verb.
practice.shortcut: being = continuous, been = perfect. Fix the word first.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Someone is auditing our accounts this week.'
options: Our accounts are been audited this week.
Our accounts are auditing this week.
Our accounts were being audited this week.
Our accounts are being audited this week.
practice.solution: Present continuous row with the vague *someone* dropped: **Our accounts are being audited this week.** 'Are been audited' misplaces been; 'are auditing' leaves the sentence active with the accounts doing the auditing; 'were being audited' shifts to the past row.
practice.shortcut: Continuous active → being + V3; drop the vague agent.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The bank offered the farmer a loan.'
options: A loan was offered the farmer by the bank.
The farmer was offered a loan by the bank.
The farmer was offer a loan by the bank.
The bank was offered a loan by the farmer.
practice.solution: The person-promoted passive is keyed: *The farmer was offered a loan by the bank.* The thing-promoted version must insert *to* ('a loan was offered **to** the farmer'); without *to* it is broken. 'Was offer a loan' lacks the participle; promoting the bank reverses who offered what.
practice.shortcut: Person promoted = no preposition. Thing promoted = needs to.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The principal awarded the topper a gold medal.'
options: A gold medal was awarded the topper by the principal.
The topper was awarded a gold medal by the principal.
The topper was awarding a gold medal by the principal.
A gold medal was awarded by the topper to the principal.
practice.solution: Promote the person: *The topper was awarded a gold medal by the principal.* The medal-promoted option is missing *to* before the topper; 'was awarding' is the wrong form after was; making the medal awarded by the topper reverses the ceremony.
practice.shortcut: Award/give/show/offer: promote the person.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'You must complete the formalities today.'
options: The formalities must been completed today.
The formalities must be completed today.
The formalities must being completed today.
The formalities must be complete today.
practice.solution: Modal row: **must + be + V3** — *The formalities must be completed today.* Nothing may sit between the modal and be: no been, no being. 'Must be complete' uses the adjective instead of the participle, so the action disappears.
practice.shortcut: Modal + be + V3, nothing else in between.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'We should respect our elders.'
options: Our elders should been respected.
Our elders should respected.
Our elders should be respected.
Our elders would be respected.
practice.solution: **Our elders should be respected** — the modal *should* is kept exactly, be follows it, and the participle closes. 'Should respected' drops be; 'would be respected' swaps the modal itself, which the key never allows.
practice.shortcut: Keep the modal, add be, close with V3.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Shut the door.'
options: Let the door be shut.
Let the door shut.
The door is shut.
Let the door been shut.
practice.solution: An order converts with **Let + object + be + V3**: *Let the door be shut.* 'Let the door shut' drops be and reads as an active permission; 'The door is shut' is a plain statement, not the order; 'been shut' cannot follow let.
practice.shortcut: Order → Let + object + be + V3.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Do not pluck the flowers in the park.'
options: The flowers are not plucked in the park.
Let the flowers not plucked in the park.
Let the flowers not be plucked in the park.
Let the flowers not being plucked in the park.
practice.solution: Negative order → **Let + object + not + be + V3**: *Let the flowers not be plucked in the park.* 'Are not plucked' turns the order into a statement; 'not plucked' drops be; 'not being plucked' breaks the slot after let.
practice.shortcut: Negative order: Let ... not be + V3.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Please do not touch the exhibits.'
options: You are requested not to touch the exhibits.
The exhibits are requested not to be touched.
You are requested to touch not the exhibits.
You are request not to touch the exhibits.
practice.solution: A polite please-sentence takes the frame **You are requested not to + V1**: *You are requested not to touch the exhibits.* Making the exhibits the requested party garbles the frame; 'to touch not' misplaces the negative; 'are request' drops the -ed.
practice.shortcut: please + not → requested not to + V1.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Never tell a lie.'
options: You are advise not to tell a lie.
You are advised not to tell a lie.
You are advised not telling a lie.
A lie is advised not to be told.
practice.solution: Advice in imperative form converts to **You are advised not to + V1**: *You are advised not to tell a lie.* 'Are advise' lacks the participle; 'not telling' replaces the infinitive with a gerund; the lie cannot be the subject of an advice frame.
practice.shortcut: Advice imperative → advised not to + V1.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Please post this letter today itself.'
options: You are requested that post this letter today itself.
This letter is requested to post today itself.
You are requested to post this letter today itself.
You are request to post this letter today itself.
practice.solution: **You are requested to post this letter today itself.** The frame requested + to + V1 swallows the please, and the rest of the sentence is carried across word for word. A that-clause after requested is ungrammatical; making the letter the requested party scrambles the frame.
practice.shortcut: Please ... → You are requested to + V1.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Kindly send the invitation card by this evening.'
options: The invitation card is requested to be sent by this evening.
You are requested to sending the invitation card by this evening.
You are requested to send the invitation card by this evening.
You are request to send the invitation card by this evening.
practice.solution: Kindly marks a request: **You are requested to send the invitation card by this evening.** The card cannot be the requested party; after to the base verb *send* is fixed — 'to sending' breaks the frame; 'are request' loses the -ed.
practice.shortcut: kindly = please → requested to + V1.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the question: 'Who invented the radio?'
options: By whom the radio was invented?
By whom was the radio invented?
Who was the radio invented?
Whom was invented the radio?
practice.solution: Who as doer → **By whom + auxiliary + subject + V3**: *By whom was the radio invented?* 'By whom the radio was invented?' is statement order — the auxiliary must precede the subject in a question; 'Who was the radio invented' scrambles the roles.
practice.shortcut: Who-questions: By whom + aux + subject + V3 + ?

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the question: 'Whom has the principal punished?'
options: Who has been punished by the principal?
Who has punished by the principal?
Who has been punish by the principal?
By whom has the principal been punished?
practice.solution: Here whom is the receiver, so the wh-word itself is promoted to subject: **Who has been punished by the principal?** — present perfect row, been + punished. 'Has punished' drops been; 'been punish' lacks the participle; the last option makes the principal the punished party.
practice.shortcut: Whom-receiver questions: the wh-word becomes the subject.
